newsitem.title: UK: Rugby Union - English union denies approach to Henry.
newsitem.headline: Rugby Union - English union denies approach to Henry.

text.p: LONDON, July 10 - England's Rugby Football Union has denied that it has made an approach to Auckland coach Graham Henry to coach its national side, NZPA reports.
Reports have linked Henry, Australian Bob Dwyer and Scot Ian McGeechan with the post currently filled by Jack Rowell.
The story, first floated in New Zealand earlier this week, hit the headlines in England on Thursday with the Daily Mail's back page saying "Rowell routed by top Kiwi".
The Mail said officials at Twickenham had "gone behind Jack Rowell's back in a bid to sign a New Zealander as their first fully professional national rugby coach".
And the Evening Standard said Henry "heads the queue to replace Rowell", and quotes Rowell saying he is aware of an offer being made to Henry.
Rowell, who assumed the job from Dick Best in 1994, has said he does not want to take on the job full time and wants to combine being a part-time England coach with his other business commitments.
The RFU wants a full-time professional coach to lead England into the 1999 World Cup, and Henry has said he has received offers from outside New Zealand.

In response to the reports, the RFU issued a weak denial that they were actively pursuing a replacement for Rowell, who has won 21 of his 28 tests but remains a focus of criticism for failing to achieve consistently high levels of performance with the side.
However, the denial was issued as evidence mounted that negotiations are indeed taking place.

Don Rutherford, the RFU's technical director, was reported to have flown to Auckland from England's training base in Sydney to meet with Henry. The Evening Standard said that Rutherford had also met with former Auckland coach Maurice Trapp.
No details of their meetings were released, but there was speculation that Rutherford had discussed details of an England deal.
The Standard quoted Rutherford saying: "Having someone like Graham involved in the coaching set-up has lots of merits. We have a number of representative teams besides the senior side."
Derek Morgan, chairman of the RFU's national playing committee, said: "No one has been asked or authorised to make approaches to any other coach.
"No formal discussions or decisions will be taken about the coaching position until after the players and team management return from Australia."
Henry's services are highly sought after his success in the NPC and Super 12. He holds ambitions as an All Black coach but is blocked by John Hart's tenure in the job.

Another problem for England is the internal struggle for control which will be fought out at the RFU's annual meeting tomorrow. The meeting will be a battle between progressives and traditionalists, with Rowell seen as a pawn caught in the crossfire.
The controversy comes as an unwelcome distraction for Rowell, the former lock forward who is in Sydney preparing his team for Saturday's one-off test against Australia.
